newsitem.title: USA: U.S. Dec industrial output seen boosting Q4 GDP.
newsitem.headline: U.S. Dec industrial output seen boosting Q4 GDP.

text.p: U.S. industrial output surged for the second month in a row in December, reinforcing the widely-held view that the economy accelerated strongly in the fourth quarter, economists said.
Industrial production expanded 0.8 percent in December as capacity utilization rose to 83.8 percent, the Federal Reserve said on Friday.
Economists in a Reuters poll last week had forecast a 0.6 percent gain in output and a utilization level of 83.5 percent.

"The production strength underscores the strength of the economy in the fourth quarter (and) with the the market's heightened fears over inflation, capacity utilization ... is troubling," said Michelle Colley Laughlin, money market economist at Prudential Securities Inc.

Much of the December industrial pickup came from manufacturing output, which jumped 1.1 percent. Manufacturing figures heavily in the overall numbers and offset a 3.3 percent decline in utilities-related output, economists said.
The report closely followed data on November international trade, which showed rising U.S. exports also lent strength to fourth-quarter gross domestic product.

"We have every indication that in the final three months of 1996 U.S. real GDP grew by at least 3.5 percent annualized, if not 4.0 percent," John Lonski, chief economist at Moody's Investors Service, told Reuters Financial Television.
Treasuries took the data in stride, since a fourth-quarter growth spurt has been priced in already, economists said.
But some analysts read signs of a Fed tightening in the tea leaves of the production data.

Capacity utilization is nearing levels historically associated with accelerating inflation, but it should not trigger alarms just yet, said Don Maude, chief U.S. economist at Scotia Capital Markets Inc.
"Usually 85.0 is your distress level, 84.0 is your concern level," Maude said.
The sharp drop in utility output last month allowed U.S. industry to operate at 83.8 percent of capacity rather than cross the "concern" threshold, Maude said.
The Fed will stay on hold at its next policy meeting on February 4-5, but not much longer, he said.
"This (report), along with other developments that will happen along the way, will probably put pressure on them to move in March," Maude said.

Those developments would have to include more dramatic signs of inflation or indications the economy continues to grow more quickly than the central bank would like in the first quarter, economists said.

The analysts disagreed about whether manufacturing could maintain its December pace over the next few months. Some said depleted inventories would require sustained production levels, while others cited lackluster holiday sales as a reason to expect a slowdown.
